As early as 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of a "smartphone monopoly."

Over the past two years, Apple has repeatedly expressed opposition to the case. According to the latest report from Bloomberg, the Department of Justice and Apple are currently in negotiations to settle the lawsuit.

Bloomberg pointed out that Apple has put forward "multiple proposals" this year in an attempt to reach a settlement with the Department of Justice:

The report also noted that although negotiations are underway, whether the Department of Justice and Apple can ultimately reach an agreement remains unknown.

The Department of Justice's antitrust lawsuit against Apple mainly revolves around five categories of iPhone user experience: super apps, cloud streaming games, third-party messaging apps, third-party smartwatches, and third-party digital wallets.

Over the past year, Apple has made substantive changes in response to some of the Department of Justice's concerns, including supporting the RCS communication standard in the "Messages" app, launching a brand-new "Mini App Partner Program" on the App Store, and relaxing restrictions on access to the iPhone NFC chip.

Whether the above changes will satisfy the Department of Justice remains unknown. As Bloomberg pointed out, political factors are also involved:

Apple and the Department of Justice have recently submitted a joint status report to the court on the progress of the case. In addition, Apple won a "discovery" dispute earlier this week, involving the Department of Justice's access to federal agency documents in the case.

9to5Mac Perspective

If Apple can reach a settlement with the Department of Justice, it would be a huge relief for John Ternus, who will take over as CEO in September.
